en: Advayavajra’s Works 23. *Amanasikārādhāra*,
edited by Mahāmahopādhyāya Hara Prasad Shastri.
1. In *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*, GOS 1927, Baroda, edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai; 2.
In *Taishō Daigaku Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Nenpō*.
Homage to the Buddha!

Regarding the term *amanasikāra*, many have fallen into error. On this point, someone says: "This is a corrupt word (*apaśabda*); in a compound, it ought to be *amanaskāra*. To this it is replied: by the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.14), because of the mention of "often" (*bahula*) here, there is no elision of the locative case (*saptamyā alug*). Thus, when an *aluk*-compound is formed, the forms *amanasikāraḥ*, *amanaskāraḥ*, *tvacisāraḥ*, *tvaksāraḥ*, and *yudhiṣṭhiraḥ* are established. Therefore, this is not a corrupt word.

Another says: "Alas! This statement is already established by its very definition; what, then, is unproven? That is not so, because it is seen in various sūtras and tantras. In the *Āryasarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāramahāyānasūtra*: "Phenomena that are not attended to (*amanasikāra*) are wholesome; phenomena that are attended to (*manasikāra*) are unwholesome. And in that same text:
"O you whose intention is non-conceptual, whose mind is non-abiding, who are without mindfulness or mental attention, and who are without support—homage be to you!"

Likewise, in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*, it is said: "A bodhisattva mahāsattva avoids all signs of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which follow various modes of appearance, by means of non-attention (*amanasikāra*). Other [details] are not written here for fear of excessive prolixity."

Now he says another thing: "This statement belongs only to the Sautrāntikas, not to the Māntrikas, because it is seen in the Sūtras. That is not so; for it is stated in the *Hevajra*, in the *Tattvapaṭala*: "In its own nature, there is neither mind (*citta*) nor mental factors (*caitasika*). Likewise: "For the entire world is cultivated by the mind, since it is not cultivated"—by which it is understood that [it is not cultivated] through non-mental-attention (*amanasikāra*).

Another says: "Even in the *tantra*, because the negative particle (*nañ*) has as its object a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), non-existence (*abhāva*) must be the expressed meaning. That is not so. A negation is of that which has been introduced [into the discussion]; it is called a non-presuppositional negation because what is presupposed is not negated. For example: "The king's wives are sun-blind" (*asūryampaśyā rājadhārāḥ*). The meaning is this: those royal wives are so well-guarded that they do not even see the sun. In this case, the non-existence of the sun is not being asserted.

What indeed is it that is prohibited for the wives of kings—that which is the viewing of the sun? Even when there is no mental attention (*amanasikāra*), that which is prohibited by the negative particle (*nañ*) is the mental attention toward the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhaka*) and so forth; it is not the mind itself. Therefore, there is no fault. When someone says, "The mental attention characterized by eternalism and nihilism is what is intended by the Blessed One," it is then said: "It is the non-mental-attention toward the mental attention of eternalism, nihilism, and so forth. By this term "non-mental-attention" (*amanasikāra*), the abandonment of all attachments is accomplished.

And so it was said by the Blessed One in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*: "For what reason, noble son, is the realm of non-conceptualization called 'non-mental-attention' (*amanasikāra*)? Because it transcends all signs of conceptualization. By this, the word "non-mental-attention" demonstrates the transcendence of all conceptualization.

Even in the case of the position of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is no fault. When it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin," what is brought is someone similar to a Brahmin, such as a Kṣatriya, and not something of a different genus, such as a mat. Here too, the establishment of consciousness as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is achieved. By this, one would abide in the doctrine of non-duality comparable to an illusion (*māyopama-advayavāda*). How, then, could there be the consequence of falling into nihilism (*ucchedavāda*)?

Alternatively, if the negative particle here is merely conventional (*vyavahāra-mātra*), then this statement must be understood as expressing two things: it does not negate existence because of the absence of illusion or true establishment, nor is it non-existence.
By this reasoning, the sense of negating transmigratory existence (*jagat*) would be undermined.

An etymological derivation is provided here: *amanasikāra* is a compound where the vowel *a* is predominant. It is a *madhyapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) compound, like *śākapārthiva* (a vegetable-loving king). By this, the meaning is that whatever constitutes mental attention (*manasikāra*), all of it is of the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Where was it stated by the Blessed One that the letter *a* is the maker of non-arising? As it is said in the *Hevajra*, in the *Mantrapaṭala*:
"The letter *a* is the mouth of all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the very beginning," and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are unarisen from the very beginning, the letter *A* is the "mouth," that is, the primary [element]. The letter *A* signifies the possession of the characteristic of non-arising (*anutpanna*). Thus, it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "The letter *A* is the foremost of all phonemes; it is of great significance, the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*).
It is indeed the great vital breath (*mahāprāṇa*), the unarisen, and devoid of verbal expression."
Alternatively, the syllable *a* here is the seed-syllable of selflessness (*nairātmya*). Thus, it is said in the *Hevajra*:
"The beginning of *ālī* is Nairātmyā.
By this, it is also stated that all mental engagement is without self and without intrinsic nature.
Alternatively—
she is conceived by the Buddhas as *dhī* (wisdom), whose intrinsic nature is the first vowel;
she herself is the Blessed Lady Prajñā through the yoga of the *utpannakrama* (completion stage).

Alternatively, "a" is the term for *prabhāsvara* (luminosity), and "mental engagement" (*manasikāra*) is the term for *svādhiṣṭhāna* (self-consecration). Thus, "non-mental-engagement" (*amanasikāra*) is that which is both "a" and mental engagement. By these terms beginning with "non-mental-engagement," there is brought about the realization of the inconceivable state of luminosity and self-consecration—the experience of the non-dual, unified flow of emptiness and compassion. The section on the basis of non-mental-engagement is completed.
